tldr: This is a research cluster, not one event: early-November papers widened prompt injection to agent memory, tool updates, task outcomes, and reasoning traces. A Nov 8 paper then argued for treating the model as untrusted, and a Nov 11 practitioner post showed agent guardrails bypassed with legal-style phrasing.
whats_new: A Nov 19 Stack Builders post takes the same containment line from the practitioner side: scope agent authorization so a successful prompt injection can do limited damage, rather than trying to block the injection itself.
why_it_matters: The thread keeps moving the defense out of the model: a guardrail that reads text can be argued with, so the control that holds is the permission boundary enforced in code around the tool call.

beats.headline: Persistent memory and tool updates open gaps beyond single-session injection
beats.summary: MemHarmBench tests cross-session injection in memory-persistent agents; the Tool Update Gap paper shows frameworks may keep trusting tools after updates.

beats.headline: SPILLWAY separates target admission from sanitization
beats.summary: Argues against putting an LLM on the decision that lets an action through, since that decision can itself be manipulated.

beats.headline: Benchmarks add task tampering, thought injection, and weight-level injection
beats.summary: Two papers extend injection past instruction override, to task outcomes and the chain-of-thought stage; IWIBench is adjacent, covering one model editing another's weights rather than prompts.

beats.headline: Paper frames injection as structural and treats the model as untrusted
beats.summary: Compares in-prompt defences (hardened prompts, spotlighting) against deterministic policy enforcement, human approval, and taint tracking, validated on open-weights models.

beats.headline: Practitioner post claims guardrail bypass using lawyerspeak
beats.summary: A write-up on defeating agent guardrails with legal-style language, the first non-paper item in the thread.

beats.headline: Practitioner guidance: scope agent authorization to limit injection damage
beats.summary: Stack Builders frames authorization, not detection, as the control that caps what an injected agent can do.

open_questions: Do the memory and tool-update attack papers ship reproducible harnesses that independent teams can run?
Does SPILLWAY's admission/sanitization split keep its robustness in independent evaluation on real agent frameworks?
Which guardrail products does the lawyerspeak bypass work against, and do their vendors confirm or patch it?
Do deterministic policy enforcement and taint tracking hold on closed frontier models, beyond the open-weights models the paper validated on?
Do agent frameworks ship per-tool, per-task scoped credentials by default, or is authorization scoping still left to each team?
take_for_builders: Give each agent task the narrowest credentials it needs and gate high-impact tool calls with deterministic policy or human approval, then add legal-register, task-tampering, memory-poisoning, and tool-version-change cases to your red-team suite.
